items.title: Introduction

sections.normalized_html: Breadth-first search (BFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that explores vertices level-by-level from a starting vertex. Edward F. Moore first formally described it in 1959. Since then, it has become helpful in network analysis, identifying the shortest paths in unweighted graphs, and identifying the connected components of a graph.
sections.readable_text: Breadth-first search (BFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that explores vertices level-by-level from a starting vertex. Edward F. Moore first formally described it in 1959. Since then, it has become helpful in network analysis, identifying the shortest paths in unweighted graphs, and identifying the connected components of a graph.

sections.normalized_html: BFS uses a queue, which follows a first-in, first-out (FIFO) structure, ensuring that the earliest inserted vertex is processed first. This allows BFS to explore vertices in a structured manner, expanding outward layer by layer. The process begins by selecting a starting vertex, and BFS is guaranteed to visit every vertex within the same connected component as that vertex in an undirected graph.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Breadth-first search (BFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that explores vertices level-by-level from a starting vertex. Edward F. Moore first formally described it in 1959. Since then, it has become helpful in network analysis, identifying the shortest paths in unweighted graphs, and identifying the connected components of a graph.

Content:
BFS uses a queue, which follows a first-in, first-out (FIFO) structure, ensuring that the earliest inserted vertex is processed first. This allows BFS to explore vertices in a structured manner, expanding outward layer by layer. The process begins by selecting a starting vertex, and BFS is guaranteed to visit every vertex within the same connected component as that vertex in an undirected graph.

Content:
The steps involved in a BFS traversal are as follows:

Content:
- Step 1: Initialize the empty queue and the empty list of visited vertices.
- Step 2: Add the starting vertex to the queue and to the list of visited vertices.
- Step 3: Pop the first vertex from the head of the queue.
- Step 4: For every unvisited neighbor of the dequeued vertex, process it and add to the list of visited vertices.
- Step 5: Repeat steps 3 and 4 until the queue is empty.

Content:
We can express the BFS algorithm using pseudocode. Pseudocode is a simplified, programming language-independent way of describing an algorithm. It uses a mix of natural language and programming concepts, helping programmers to plan and visualize code logic without focusing on syntax.

Content:
The pseudocode for the breadth-first search algorithm is the following:

Content:
> Initialize the empty queue and the list of visited vertices
>
> def BFS(v): # Breadth-First Search starting from v
>
> Add the starting vertex v to queue and to visited
>
> while (queue is not empty): # Continue until the queue is empty
>
> Pop vertex w from the head of the queue
>
> for (u adjacent to w): # Go over all neighbors of w
>
> if (u not in visited):
>
> Add u to visited
>
> Add u to the end of the queue

Content:
Before we continue, please note the following:

Content:
- In general, a BFS traversal is not unique, even for the same starting vertex, because multiple vertices can be added to the queue at any given step.
- To avoid ambiguity, we will fix the order of the vertices before proceeding with the algorithm. Given a choice of two or more vertices to add to the queue, we will always add the vertex with the smallest index first.
- Please note that, in practical applications, such as writing a BFS program on a computer, fixing the order of the vertices is unnecessary. If given a choice, we can select a vertex at random.

sections.normalized_html:
Breadth-first search (BFS) is an algorithm that systematically explores a graph by starting at a source node and discovering all its directly connected neighbors. Then, it lists and visits these neighbors, layer by layer, until all reachable nodes have been visited.

The pseudocode for the breadth-first search algorithm is the following:

Initialize the empty queue and the list of visited vertices

def BFS(v): # Breadth-First Search starting from v

Add the starting vertex v to the queue and to visited

while (queue is not empty): # Until the queue is not empty

Pop vertex w from the head of the queue

for (u adjacent to w): # Go over all neighbors of w

if (u not in visited):

Add u to visited

Add u to the end of the queue

So, at the next step of the breadth-first search algorithm, we pop (i.e., remove) the vertex from the head (i.e., the front) of the queue. This would be the vertex [MATH: v_1.]

Next, we traverse all the vertices that are adjacent to [MATH: v_1.] So, we add [MATH: v_{2}] to the list of visited vertices and push them into the end of the queue.

Breadth-first search (BFS) is an algorithm that systematically explores a graph by starting at a source node and discovering all its directly connected neighbors. Then, it lists and visits these neighbors, layer by layer, until all reachable nodes have been visited.

The pseudocode for the breadth-first search algorithm is the following:

Initialize the empty queue and the list of visited vertices

def BFS(v): # Breadth-First Search starting from v

Add the starting vertex v to queue and to visited

while (queue is not empty): # Continue until the queue is empty

Pop vertex w from the head of the queue

for (u adjacent to w): # Go over all neighbors of w

if (u not in visited):

Add u to visited

Add u to the end of the queue

With that in mind, we proceed as follows:

Step 1.

Push [MATH: v_5] to the end of the queue and add it to visited vertices.

Visited:

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Breadth-first search (BFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that explores vertices level-by-level from a starting vertex. Edward F. Moore first formally described it in 1959. Since then, it has become helpful in network analysis, identifying the shortest paths in unweighted graphs, and identifying the connected components of a graph.

Content:
BFS uses a queue, which follows a first-in, first-out (FIFO) structure, ensuring that the earliest inserted vertex is processed first. This allows BFS to explore vertices in a structured manner, expanding outward layer by layer. The process begins by selecting a starting vertex, and BFS is guaranteed to visit every vertex within the same connected component as that vertex in an undirected graph.

Content:
The steps involved in a BFS traversal are as follows:

Content:
- Step 1: Initialize the empty queue and the empty list of visited vertices.
- Step 2: Add the starting vertex to the queue and to the list of visited vertices.
- Step 3: Pop the first vertex from the head of the queue.
- Step 4: For every unvisited neighbor of the dequeued vertex, process it and add to the list of visited vertices.
- Step 5: Repeat steps 3 and 4 until the queue is empty.

Content:
We can express the BFS algorithm using pseudocode. Pseudocode is a simplified, programming language-independent way of describing an algorithm. It uses a mix of natural language and programming concepts, helping programmers to plan and visualize code logic without focusing on syntax.

Content:
The pseudocode for the breadth-first search algorithm is the following:

Content:
> Initialize the empty queue and the list of visited vertices
>
> def BFS(v): # Breadth-First Search starting from v
>
> Add the starting vertex v to queue and to visited
>
> while (queue is not empty): # Continue until the queue is empty
>
> Pop vertex w from the head of the queue
>
> for (u adjacent to w): # Go over all neighbors of w
>
> if (u not in visited):
>
> Add u to visited
>
> Add u to the end of the queue

Content:
Before we continue, please note the following:

Content:
- In general, a BFS traversal is not unique, even for the same starting vertex, because multiple vertices can be added to the queue at any given step.
- To avoid ambiguity, we will fix the order of the vertices before proceeding with the algorithm. Given a choice of two or more vertices to add to the queue, we will always add the vertex with the smallest index first.
- Please note that, in practical applications, such as writing a BFS program on a computer, fixing the order of the vertices is unnecessary. If given a choice, we can select a vertex at random.

Content:
Let's look at how to apply BFS to a concrete graph.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
Let's apply the breadth-first search algorithm to the graph below, starting at [MATH: v_3.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7c2411ea43a9e46b673b73e4c5beee97]

Content:
First, let's fix the following order of vertices.
[MATH: v_1, \: v_2,\: v_3,\: v_4, \: v_5, \: v_6]

Content:
Now, we proceed as follows:

Content:
| Step 1. |
| [IMG: /graphics/b43e13032c07f1e6f5d692ef2bb53dbf] | | Push [MATH: v_3] to the end of the queue and add it to visited vertices. | / | | Queue: | [MATH: v_3] | / | Visited: | [MATH: v_3] | | |
| Step 2. |
| [IMG: /graphics/438c5aec7feb63ba2f11811b9cc7a2ca] | | Pop [MATH: v_3] from the head of the queue, visit its unvisited neighbors [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_5] and push them to the end of the queue. / / Watch out! Notice that the vertex [MATH: v_2] goes first since it has a smaller index. | / | | Queue: | [MATH: v_2,] [MATH: v_5] | / | Visited: | [MATH: v_3,] [MATH: v_2,] [MATH: v_5] | | |
| Step 3. |
| [IMG: /graphics/1044e95fa058451897716498c3ad7ed4] | | Pop [MATH: v_2] from the head of the queue, visit its unvisited neighbors [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_4] and push them to the end of the queue. / / Watch out! Notice that the vertex [MATH: v_1] goes first since it has a smaller index. | / | | Queue: | [MATH: v_5,] [MATH: v_1,] [MATH: v_4] | / | Visited: | [MATH: v_3,] [MATH: v_2,] [MATH: v_5,] [MATH: v_1,] [MATH: v_4] | | |
| Steps 4-6. |
| ... | | Since all the vertices have been visited, in the next steps, we pop the remaining vertices from the head of the queue in the following order: / [MATH: v_5,] [MATH: v_1,] [MATH: v_4] | / | | Queue: | | / | Visited: | [MATH: v_3,] [MATH: v_2,] [MATH: v_5,] [MATH: v_1,] [MATH: v_4] | | |

Content:
And we're done. The BFS algorithm is complete, and the list of visited vertices, in the order they're visited, are as follows:

Content:
[MATH: v_3,\quad v_2,\quad v_5,\quad v_1,\quad v_4]
